item.title: Macklem says inflation forecast is lower, but oil price pressures are lingering
item.description: Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem says falling global oil prices could mean inflation ends the year below the central bank’s last forecast.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem says falling global oil prices could mean inflation ends the year below the central bank’s last forecast. The Bank of Canada said back in October that it saw inflation rising to 3.5 per cent by the end of the year as stubbornly high global oil prices threatened to put more pressure on consumers. Statistics Canada said inflation held steady at 3.1 per cent in October. High gas prices from war in the Middle East continued to be the biggest driver of inflation, but the agency said upward pressure was broad-based across groceries and clothing as well. Macklem suggested at a press conference in Toronto on Tuesday that recent relief at the gas pumps should mean inflation holds around those levels through the end of the year. “The inflation forecast is a bit lower. Those costs that built up over the previous eight months, they’re still there, but there’s a bit of edge (that’s) come off the inflation forecast,” he said. The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by a quarter point to 2.5 per cent in October as it warned gas prices were staying higher for longer than first expected and inflationary pressures could start to spread. Officials signalled at the time that they’d “proceed carefully,” but there could be a need for more rate hikes to come. Macklem also addressed the current inflation outlook in a speech to the Economic Club of Canada in Toronto on Tuesday. While he acknowledged the recent climbdown in global benchmark oil prices, he said that wasn’t the only factor monetary policymakers were weighing. “So far, businesses have largely absorbed the higher production and transport costs. But historical lags and our own business surveys suggest more pass-through to consumer prices in the year ahead. This second-round effect of the oil shock will add to inflation persistence,” he said in prepared remarks. CIBC chief economist Avery Shenfeld said in a note to clients on Tuesday that the governor seemed to be downplaying the disinflationary impact of falling oil prices. Shenfeld said Macklem’s focus on lingering inflation risks suggests the central bank could be gearing up to deliver a second consecutive rate hike at its next decision on Dec. 9. “There was no direct reference to the December meeting, but what was apparent was that the governor was going out of his way to not show any changes in his thinking from October whenever possible,” he said. Odds of a quarter-point hike from the Bank of Canada next month stood at 79 per cent as of Tuesday, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. That’s up from nearly 63 per cent on Monday. Macklem said Tuesday the Bank of Canada will be weighing next week’s releases of gross domestic product data for the third quarter and November labour market figures before deciding what to do at its final policy rate decision of the year. --- Craig Lord, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

item.title: Global stocks are mixed as AI shares tumble after a retreat on Wall Street
item.description: World stocks were mixed on Wednesday after a wave of heavy selling of stocks linked to artificial intelligence once again hit Wall Street.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: HONG KONG — World stocks were mixed on Wednesday after a wave of heavy selling of stocks linked to artificial intelligence once again hit Wall Street. U.S. futures slipped and oil prices also fell. Relief over Nvidia’s decision to restore Jensen Huang as its CEO has been tempered by questions over the chipmaker’s corporate governance and President Donald Trump’s influence. In early European trading, Germany’s DAX was up 0.1 per cent to 25,046.66. In Paris, the CAC 40 rose 1 per cent to 8,120.72, while Britain’s FTSE 100 gained 0.5 per cent to 10,515.74. The future for the S&P 500 was 0.8 per cent lower, while the future for the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.3 per cent. In Asian trading, Taiwan’s Taiex tumbled 5 per cent as AI chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. sank 3.6 per cent. Chip designer Mediatek plunged 10 per cent. In South Korea, the Kospi lost 6.2 per cent to 4,697.51 as Samsung Electronics fell 9.9 per cent. SK Hynix plummeted 11.1 per cent. Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 dropped 2.8 per cent to 57,011.62. Shares of OpenAI investor SoftBank Group slumped 14.8 per cent and semiconductor maker Kioxia plunged 14.2 per cent. The Hang Seng in Hong Kong slipped 1.1 per cent to 21,966.01. The Shanghai Composite index declined 2 per cent to 3,476.47, falling to its lowest level in more than a year. The Trump administration is expected to soon announce plans to raise tariffs on China and 15 other trading partners. China recorded a record trade surplus of nearly US$1.2 trillion last year. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 edged 0.4 per cent lower to 8,692.40. The consumer price index in October rose to 4.9 per cent from a year earlier, topping expectations. That could put pressure on the central bank to raise interest rates. India’s Sensex rose 1.5 per cent. On Tuesday, stocks tied to the artificial intelligence industry dragged the U.S. market lower after a surge the day before quickly fizzled. That’s even though much of the rest of Wall Street rose, along with confidence among Americans in the economy. The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent to its eighth loss in the last nine days. The Nasdaq composite shed 1.5 per cent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.9 per cent. They’re the latest swings for a market that’s been mostly sinking since hitting its all-time high last month. The surprise return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO, announced Monday, does bring back a charismatic leader who championed the entire AI industry. But it does not settle deeper concerns such as whether AI can possibly produce enough profit and productivity to justify massive investments in data centers. High interest rates are making it more difficult to borrow money to pay for the industry’s growth. Sweeping victories for Democrats earlier this month in the U.S. midterm elections, meanwhile, have raised the possibility of more regulation for AI, potentially slowing construction of data centers. Nvidia fell 5.9 per cent a day after soaring 31.5 per cent to its biggest gain in more than two decades. Other stocks around the AI industry fell by similar amounts. And Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sank 6.5 per cent to drop below $83. That’s how much Anthropic first sold its stock for in its initial public offering last week. The stock had briefly jumped as high as $115 in its first day of trading amid a frenzy of hype. Such drops were powerful enough to drag the S&P 500 index lower even though most of the stocks within the index climbed. They rose following the latest report to say confidence among U.S. consumers is improving by more than economists expected. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, climbed 2.4 per cent to $88.78. It’s been yo-yoing between $72 and $114 since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. Early Wednesday, Brent was down 1.5 per cent to $87.43 a barrel. U.S. benchmark crude oil dropped 1.8 per cent to $80.56 per barrel. The U.S. dollar rose to 159.42 Japanese yen from 159.26 yen. The euro slid to US$1.0944 from $1.0966. Elaine Lai, The Associated Press

item.title: Oil money helped N.L.'s debt, but experts say the province still needs a plan
item.description: An oil windfall has helped the Newfoundland and Labrador government reduce its sizable debt, but some experts say the province still needs a long-term plan to pay off the balance.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: ST. JOHN’S — An oil windfall has helped the Newfoundland and Labrador government reduce its sizable debt, but some experts say the province still needs a long-term plan to pay off the balance. A comparison of budgets and financial updates across Canada shows Newfoundland and Labrador’s per-capita net debt is expected to be the highest among the provinces for the current fiscal year, which ends in March. Economist Wade Locke said the provincial government would have to have a budget surplus of roughly $350 million a year for the next three decades to bring its per-capita net debt down to the Canadian average. That’s assuming a constant interest rate of about 3.6 per cent, he said in an interview Tuesday. “The problem is so massive. It’s going to require a huge effort and a well laid-out plan,” said Locke, a retired professor at Memorial University. “It’s not just a matter of picking numbers off a spreadsheet.” That plan should include changes to legislation requiring subsequent governments to follow through with it, particularly since reigning in spending and reducing debt are not popular policies, he added. Newfoundland and Labrador’s Progressive Conservative government delivered an economic update on Monday projecting a surplus of $78 million at the end of the 2026-27 fiscal year and a reduced net debt. It was a sharp contrast to the budget tabled in April which forecast a $688 million deficit. The province’s net debt is now expected to reach $19.3 billion by the end of March, rather than the $20.8 billion laid out in the budget. About $1.2 billion — or just under 10 per cent of the province’s entire budget — will have to pay for debt servicing costs, including interest. Government officials said the new numbers were driven by nearly $1.5 billion in extra revenue, most of which comes from the soaring oil prices that followed military strikes against Iran by the U.S. and Israel earlier this year. Newfoundland and Labrador is home to four offshore oil installations, and production is up at all of them, Craig Pardy, the province’s finance minister, told reporters in St. John’s on Monday. Pardy had previously promised to deliver a debt management plan with his fall fiscal update. On Monday, he announced a $175-million investment into a new sinking fund, which officials said would mature to $750 million by 2052 and be used to pay off debt. Locke noted the sinking fund money would only cover about four per cent of what the province currently owes. Pardy said Monday that the province’s gross domestic product is expected to grow this fiscal year by 7.1 per cent, a number that leads the country. He also pointed to possible returns from Equinor’s proposed Bay du Nord offshore oil project and a new energy agreement with Quebec, neither of which have been finalized. But Renaud Brossard said the anticipated economic activity may not be enough to counter some of the headwinds facing the province. One in four people in Newfoundland and Labrador are 65 or older, and seniors tend to pay fewer taxes and need more health care, said Brossard, who is the vice president of communications for the Montreal Economic Institute think tank “There absolutely needs to be a debt management plan,” Brossard said in an interview. In a news release Tuesday, the Canadian Taxpayers Federation applauded the Newfoundland and Labrador government’s move to squirrel away much of its oil windfall rather than spend it. Both Locke and Brossard had similar praise. However, in an email, Devin Drover, the federation’s Atlantic director, acknowledged Pardy’s fiscal update on Monday delivered debt reduction, but not a “debt management plan per se.” “Taxpayers still owe … over $19 billion, and that bill comes due whether oil prices co-operate or not,” Drover said. He suggested the province introduce legislation requiring that windfall money be used to pay off debt. He also said the province needs to make clear debt-reduction targets and reign in spending. “If the government locks that in, this year’s progress becomes a turning point instead of a one-off,” Drover said. The previous Liberal government introduced a “future fund” with mandatory annual contributions to help pay off debt. The Progressive Conservatives axed the annual requirement rules earlier this year, saying it didn’t make sense to borrow more for the fund. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

item.title: Drops for Nvidia, Anthropic and other AI stocks drag the U.S. market back down
item.description: HONG KONG — Global stocks were mixed Tuesday after a rally on Wall Street as Jensen Huang returned as Nvidia’s CEO. U.S. futures edged higher. Oil prices extended their losses, falling close to their ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence industry dragged the U.S. market lower Tuesday after their surge from the day before quickly fizzled. That’s even though much of the rest of Wall Street rose, along with confidence among Americans in the economy. The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent to its eighth loss in the last nine days. Tech stocks once again led the way and yanked the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 1.5 per cent. Stocks outside of AI held up much better, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 423 points, or 0.9 per cent. They’re the latest swings for a market that’s been mostly sinking since hitting its all-time high last month. The worry is that prices for AI-related stocks shot too high into a possible bubble and need to deflate. That carries immense consequences for the broader market and workers’ 401(k) accounts because AI companies have grown into Wall Street’s most influential stocks. While the surprise return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO announced Monday does bring back a charismatic leader who championed the entire AI industry, it does not settle the deep concerns dogging it. For one, doubts remain about whether AI can possibly produce enough profit and productivity to make the massive investments underway in data centres worth it. At the same time, high interest rates make it more difficult to borrow money to pay for the industry’s growth. Sweeping victories for Democrats earlier this month in the U.S. midterm elections, meanwhile, have raised concerns about more regulation for AI, including possible halts to further construction of data centres. To be sure, AI stocks and the broader U.S. market have been prone to extreme reversals since the summer, not only week to week but even hour to hour. For now, at least, the momentum is back downward. Nvidia fell 5.9 per cent a day after soaring 31.5 per cent to its biggest gain in more than two decades. Other stocks around the AI industry fell by similar amounts. CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and rents out access to them over the cloud, tumbled 11.8 per cent. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centres, dropped 4.8 per cent. And Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sank 6.5 per cent to drop below US$83. That’s how much Anthropic first sold its stock for in its initial public offering last week. The stock had briefly jumped as high as US$115 in its first day of trading amid a frenzy of hype. Such drops were powerful enough to drag the S&P 500 index lower even though most of the stocks within the index climbed. They rose following the latest report to say confidence among U.S. consumers is improving by more than economists expected. Confidence jumped sharply for Democrats and independents following the midterm election results, according to the Conference Board. That narrowed the wide gap between them and Republicans, whose confidence fell slightly. The results echo a report from the University of Michigan released earlier in the month, which also showed a rise in overall sentiment following the midterm elections and a drop in oil prices from late October. Companies in industries across the economy, meanwhile, continue to report strong growth in profits for the summer. Dollar Tree climbed 11.2 per cent after reporting bigger earnings for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The average shopper spent slightly more in its stores during the three months than they did in last year’s third quarter, and more of them came in than last year. Kohl’s rallied 19.5 per cent after reporting a profit for the latest quarter, when analysts were expecting basically zero. It also gave forecasts for revenue for the final three months of its fiscal year that were better than expected. Businesses in the S&P 500 are on pace to report overall growth in earnings per share of more than 25 per cent for a third straight quarter, according to FactSet. That’s a big deal because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits and interest rates over the long term. But emotions of investors can also overwhelm them in the short term, as the last few weeks have demonstrated. All told, the S&P 500 fell 36.08 points to 7,201.09. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 423.39 to 50,018.70, and the Nasdaq composite fell 356.02 to 23,733.54. In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.93 per cent from 4.92 per cent late Monday after drifting up and down earlier in the day. Oil prices rose, which tend to push upward on inflation and on bond yields. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil climbed 2.4 per cent to US$88.78. It’s been yo-yoing between US$72 and US$114 since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 6.3 per cent, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 rallied 3.9 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves, as they caught up to Monday’s surge from Wall Street. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Writer Elaine Lai contributed to this report
